iterations.output_text:
# KV Cache: A Technical Overview

## What Is KV Cache?

KV cache is an optimization technique used in transformer-based language models to avoid redundant computation during autoregressive generation. In transformers, each token's representation depends on all previous tokens through self-attention, which requires computing attention scores between the current token and every preceding token. As sequences grow longer, recomputing these attention operations from scratch for every new token becomes computationally expensive—specifically, attention calculations scale quadratically with sequence length.

KV cache addresses this by caching the computed key and value matrices from previously processed tokens. When generating a new token, instead of recalculating keys and values for the entire context, the model retrieves the cached keys and values while only computing the new token's query vector and its interaction with the existing cache. This transforms the per-token computational complexity from O(n) attention operations down to essentially O(1) for the historical context.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

Long context inference presents unique challenges that make KV caching essential. Without caching, generating a response for a 100,000-token document would require quadratic-time attention computations at every step, making real-time inference impractical. KV cache enables linear-time generation relative to output length rather than input length.

Beyond raw performance, KV cache unlocks several practical capabilities. Models can maintain coherent conversations across extended interactions without degrading latency. Techniques like retrieval-augmented generation become viable when the full context must persist throughout reasoning. Memory-efficient fine-tuning approaches such as LoRA benefit because cache management reduces the memory footprint during inference.

However, KV cache introduces trade-offs around memory consumption and implementation
